This bill would update Australian customs law to reflect changes to the free trade agreement with Singapore.
It would create new rules for deciding which goods from Singapore qualify for lower tariffs, and set out how to claim that treatment.
The new rules would replace the existing framework after a three-year transition period, and the changes would start on the later of royal assent or the amendment agreement's entry into force.
Introduce new rules of origin for goods imported from Singapore.
Introduce new procedures for claiming preferential tariff treatment for Singaporean originating goods.
Extend record keeping obligations for Australian originating goods exported to Singapore.
Importers and exporters of goods between Australia and Singapore.

The majority voted in favour of the bills' main idea. In parliamentary jargon, they voted to read the bills for a [second time](https://www.peo.gov.au/learning/fact-sheets/making-a-law.html). ### What is the main idea of the bills? The bills make the changes *"necessary as a result of recently agreed changes to the rules of origin in the [Singapore‑Australia Free Trade Agreement](http://dfat.gov.au/trade/agreements/safta/Pages/singapore-australia-fta.aspx) (SAFTA)"*. Read more in the [bills digest](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd1718a/18bd041).

The bill implements amendments to the Customs Act to give effect to the updated Singapore-Australia Free Trade Agreement, which serves as the economic pillar of the Comprehensive Strategic Partnership announced in June 2015. The changes introduce simplified rules of origin, improve market access for services such as law and financial services, and build on an 80% increase in bilateral trade and 350% rise in investment since the original 2003 agreement.

The speaker moved the second reading of the Customs Tariff Amendment (Singapore-Australia Free Trade Agreement Amendment Implementation) Bill 2017, which amends the Customs Tariff Act to implement the amended agreement by providing duty-free access for most eligible goods, adjusting concessional items, and inserting a new schedule for excise-equivalent rates on alcohol, tobacco, and fuel, with a three-year transition period before repealing the old provisions.

Labor supported the Customs Amendment (Singapore-Australia Free Trade Agreement Amendment Implementation) Bill 2017 and cognate bill, but criticised the Turnbull government for waiving labour market testing for contractual service suppliers and for a lack of transparency and independent economic modelling. The two-way trade between Australia and Singapore was valued at $22.7 billion in 2016.

The Customs Amendment Bill introduces new product-specific rules of origin and self-certification to simplify administration and reduce compliance costs for traders under the Singapore-Australia Free Trade Agreement. The upgraded agreement also includes mutual recognition of professional qualifications, a raised Foreign Investment Review Board screening threshold to $1,094 million for private Singaporean investment, and new visa arrangements for longer stays.

The Customs Amendment (Singapore-Australia Free Trade Agreement Amendment Implementation) Bill 2017 was supported, with Singapore’s free trade success contrasted against Venezuela’s economic collapse (460% inflation, -8% growth, 21,000 murders) to argue for the agreement’s benefits in education, legal accreditation, and financial services.

The speaker supported the Customs Amendment Bill for the Singapore-Australia Free Trade Agreement, highlighting tariff removal and market access for goods and services from their south-west Western Australia electorate, including wine, lamb, beef, marron, abalone, chocolate, olive oil, cheeses, and fudge, as well as opportunities for education, irrigation, and professional services via the upgraded Busselton-Margaret River Airport.

Labor supported the Customs Amendment and Customs Tariff Amendment bills to implement the second update to the Singapore-Australia Free Trade Agreement, which provides duty-free access for most goods, updates rules of origin, restricts ISDS mechanisms with public welfare exemptions, and recognises Australian qualifications. However, Labor opposed the removal of labour market testing for contractual service suppliers, arguing it contradicts the government's earlier commitment to mandatory testing.

The speaker supported the Customs Amendment bills to implement the updated Singapore-Australia Free Trade Agreement (SAFTA), citing $4.8 billion in services exports to Singapore in 2016 and criticizing the member for Herbert for not contributing to the debate on the deal's benefits for Townsville.
Customs Amendment (Singapore-Australia Free Trade Agreement Amendment Implementation) Act 2017

In parliamentary jargon, they voted to read the bill for a third time. ### What is this bill's main idea? According to the [bills digest](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd1718a/18bd027), the purpose of the bill was: > *to amend the International Monetary Agreements Act 1947 (the IMA Act) to provide a standing appropriation and authority to borrow for payments to meet drawings made by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) under the decision to renew the New Arrangements to Borrow (NAB) for a further five years, from 17 November 2017.*

The opposition supported the International Monetary Agreements Amendment (New Arrangements to Borrow) Bill 2017, which renews Australia’s lending commitment to the IMF under the New Arrangements to Borrow (NAB) for five years from 17 November 2017 to 16 November 2022, with a maximum commitment of SDR 2.22 billion (approximately A$4.05 billion). The speaker argued the bill is timely and pressing, facilitating expeditious passage, and noted it has no direct budget impact but represents a contingent liability.

The Australian government introduced the Broadcasting Legislation Amendment (Broadcasting Reform) Bill 2017 to modernise media regulation, including repealing broadcasting licence fees and datacasting charges, abolishing the 75% audience reach rule and the two-out-of-three cross-media control rule, and extending anti-siphoning reforms, with a $4.6 million annual transitional support package for 19 broadcasters. The bill also increases local content obligations for regional television licensees following a trigger event and is part of a broader reform package announced on 6 May 2017, supported unanimously by the media industry.

The Commercial Broadcasting (Tax) Bill 2017 introduces a new spectrum tax to replace broadcasting licence fees, raising about $40 million annually and providing overall fee relief for broadcasters, with regional broadcasters paying significantly less based on transmitter power and spectrum use. The bill is part of the government's Broadcast and Content Reform Package, has unanimous industry support, and is contingent on the passage of the Broadcasting Reform Bill.

Labor supported the majority of the broadcasting reform bills but opposed repealing the two-out-of-three cross-media rule, warning it would worsen Australia’s already high media ownership concentration and harm diversity, and criticised the government’s piecemeal approach for lacking holistic, evidence-based reform.

The speaker argued for the Broadcasting Legislation Amendment (Broadcasting Reform) Bill 2017, which abolishes the 75 per cent reach rule and the two-out-of-three cross-media rule, introduces higher local content obligations for regional commercial television licensees after ownership changes, and abolishes broadcasting licence fees while maintaining other diversity rules and the anti-siphoning list for major sporting events.

The speaker argued against repealing the two-out-of-three rule, which limits media owners to two of three platforms (radio, TV, newspaper) in a market, citing that Murdoch-owned titles account for 64.2% of metropolitan circulation and Fairfax 26.4%, and that further concentration would harm democratic diversity. They supported other measures in the bill, including licence fee relief, but opposed removing the ownership restriction.

The speaker argued that the Broadcasting Legislation Amendment (Broadcasting Reform) Bill 2017 is necessary to modernise Australian media law, citing the 90% decline in Prime Media's value over a decade and a 14% drop in newspaper advertising in 2016, and supported abolishing the two-out-of-three and 75% ownership rules, reducing broadcast licence fees, banning gambling ads during children's sports broadcasts, revising the antisiphoning list, and providing a $30 million package for women's and niche sports on subscription TV.

The government argued that the Broadcasting Legislation Amendment Bill 2017 and Commercial Broadcasting (Tax) Bill 2017 will abolish broadcasting licence fees, introduce a spectrum tax, and remove the 75% audience reach rule and two-out-of-three rule while maintaining protections for local content and competition, with the package having unanimous media industry support.
The Commercial Broadcasting (Tax) Bill 2017 supports the Broadcasting Legislation Amendment (Broadcasting Reform) Bill 2017, particularly regarding spectrum fees, and was commended to the House.

Labor will not oppose the two amendments to the Broadcasting Legislation Amendment (Broadcasting Reform) Bill 2017 concerning programming requirements and trigger events, but argued the government’s media reform deal was made behind closed doors, citing 61% voter disapproval, $30 million in taxpayer-funded handouts to Fox Sports, and unanswered questions about a journalism innovation fund.

The speaker argued that the Broadcasting Legislation Amendment Bill 2017 is opposed by 61% of Australians and will cause job losses in regional Australia, not job creation. They criticised government deals with crossbenchers, including a $60 million fund for the Nick Xenophon Team and a competitive neutrality inquiry targeting the ABC.

The speaker argued that the Broadcasting Legislation Amendment (Broadcasting Reform) Bill 2017 is urgently needed to help Australian media businesses compete with global internet companies, and criticised the shadow minister for opposing the reforms with illogical arguments, including a claim that industry support for the bill disqualified it.

It says that the minister must cause a copy of the report be tabled in each house of parliament within 15 sitting days of that house after its receipt by the minister and that the minister must cause a copy of the report to be published on the internet within 30 days after its receipt by the minister.* ### Amendment text > *(12) Clause 53, page 28 (after line 13), at the end of the clause, add:* > >> *(4) The Minister must cause a copy of the report to be tabled in each House of Parliament within 15 sitting days of that House after its receipt by the Minister.* >> >> *(5) The Minister must cause a copy of the report to be published on the internet within 30 days after its receipt by the Minister.*

The majority voted in favour of a [motion](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2018-02-06.12.3) that the bill as amended by agreed to. This vote ends the in Committee stage of considering the bill, which is the stage when senators propose and vote on possible amendments. Now the senators will decide whether to read the bill for a third time, which is parliamentary jargon for agreeing to pass the bill. ### What does this bill do? The bill will deliver on a [2016 election commitment](http://www.abc.net.au/news/rural/2016-06-23/barnaby-joyce-agriculture-election/7535450) by creating the Regional Investment Corporation. The Corporation will, among other things, *"administer farm business loans and financial assistance granted to states and territories in relation to water infrastructure projects"*. Read more in the [bills digest](http://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd1718a/18bd013).

The majority voted in favour of passing [the bill](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/r5906), with amendments. In parliamentary jargon, they voted to read the bill [for a third time](https://www.peo.gov.au/learning/fact-sheets/making-a-law.html). The bill will now be sent back to the House of Representatives where our Members of Parliament (MPs) will decide whether they agree with the Senate's amendments. ### What does this bill do? This bill delivers on a 2016 election commitment and creates the Regional Investment Corporation *"to administer farm business loans and financial assistance granted to states and territories in relation to water infrastructure projects"*. More information about the bill is available in its [bills digest](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd1718a/18bd013).

The speaker argued that the Regional Investment Corporation Bill 2017 represents bad policy, a "boondoggle" and "pork barrel" designed to recover Nationals party votes in Orange, and moved a second reading amendment seconded by the member for Whitlam on grounds of ministerial accountability.

The speaker supported the Regional Investment Corporation Bill 2017, rejecting an amendment by the member for Hunter, Mr Fitzgibbon, and praised Agriculture Minister Barnaby Joyce's record. The speech cited over 1,200 farming businesses accessing $670 million in low-interest concessional loans, $250 million a year in farm business loans, $200 million for biosecurity, free trade agreements with Japan, South Korea and China, and progress on food labelling laws and the wine equalisation tax.
The speaker argued that the member for Murray (Barnaby Joyce) should address questions about his legitimacy to serve as a minister and MP, rather than listing his achievements.

The speaker opposed the Regional Investment Corporation Bill 2017, arguing it was a pork-barrelling exercise that favoured National Party interests. They criticised the choice of Orange over Bendigo, citing Bendigo's existing rural finance expertise from Bendigo Bank and Rural Finance, and claimed the government failed to consult stakeholders or conduct proper research.

The speaker argued that the Regional Investment Corporation Bill 2017 would streamline delivery of up to $2 billion in concessional farm loans and a $2 billion National Water Infrastructure Loan Facility, citing $725 million in farm business loans already approved. They also announced government investments in Geelong including the NDIA headquarters, the Australian Bureau of Statistics National Data Acquisition Centre, $50 million for the Great Ocean Road, and $224 million for regional rail upgrades.

The speaker supported the Regional Investment Corporation Bill 2017, announcing the $4 billion RIC will open by July 2018 in Orange, NSW, to deliver farm business and water infrastructure loans more efficiently, with $2 billion in concessional loans and $725 million already approved to 1,340 farm businesses, while criticising Labor for opposing the RIC and for turning its back on regional communities.

The speaker argued the Regional Investment Corporation Bill 2017 would deliver up to $4 billion in concessional loans for farm businesses and water infrastructure, noting $680 million already approved to 1,275 farms. They also highlighted record farm production value of $62.8 billion in 2016–17 and detailed specific water infrastructure commitments including $130 million for Rookwood Weir and feasibility studies for Bundaberg Channel and Gayndah irrigation projects.

The speaker opposed the Regional Investment Corporation Bill 2017, citing three objections: the bill was introduced by Deputy Prime Minister Barnaby Joyce, who may be ineligible due to dual citizenship with New Zealand; the bill lacked cost-benefit analysis and raised stakeholder concerns about its flawed structure; and it failed to address growing inequality between capital cities and regional areas. The speaker supported an amendment by the member for Hunter.

The speech supported the amendment to the Regional Investment Corporation Bill, arguing the proposed $4 billion corporation would duplicate existing state and territory loan schemes and serve political rather than regional interests. It also criticised Deputy Prime Minister Barnaby Joyce’s invalid citizenship status and the National Party’s record, including dam proposals in Tyalgum and Byrill Creek and the APVMA relocation.

Climate change is the greatest challenge facing Australian farmers, with the Garnaut review predicting unchecked climate change would destroy 98% of Murray-Darling Basin farmland, and the government's emissions reduction fund is underfunded and ineffective.

The speech opposed the Regional Investment Corporation Bill 2017, arguing it lacks a coherent policy rationale and accountability, with a $4 billion fund to be overseen by a three-person board and the corporation located in Orange without a proper process. It also criticised the Deputy Prime Minister for neglecting Tasmanian farmers and visiting the state only once.

The speaker argued that the Regional Investment Corporation Bill 2017 should be passed to replace state-administered farm concessional loans with a nationally consistent system, citing a National Audit Office report that found South Australia’s processing costs reached $416,000 per successful application and that only $8 million of $15 million in dairy recovery loans was allocated, with six of 14 applications rejected. He called on the Nick Xenophon Team to unconditionally support the bill.

The speaker opposed the Regional Investment Corporation Bill 2017, arguing that similar Turnbull government loan schemes like the Northern Australia Infrastructure Fund have failed to deliver any projects, and that the new $81 million scheme lacks cost-benefit analysis, will not benefit North Queensland, and should be located in the Burdekin rather than Orange.

Supported the Regional Investment Corporation Bill 2017, arguing for nationally consistent farm loan schemes after noting South Australia received only $17.2 million (2%) of $724 million in concessional loans. Also called for the Deputy Prime Minister to step aside from the water portfolio over alleged Murray-Darling Basin water theft and backed decentralisation with broader policy.

The speaker argued in support of the Regional Investment Corporation Bill 2017, opposing the member for Hunter's amendment, and highlighted government policies such as the instant write-off for water and fencing, the $20,000 instant asset write-off, farm management deposits up to $8,000, and the Inland Rail project as beneficial to farmers and regional communities. The speaker also urged caution regarding accusations from the Four Corners program, stressing that investigations should conclude before action is taken.

The speaker argued that the Regional Investment Corporation Bill grants the Minister for Agriculture and Water Resources excessive, non-disallowable control over $4 billion in loans and the corporation's mandate, risking pork-barrelling and political bias, while noting the $81.4 million cost and criticising the minister’s handling of the Murray-Darling Basin and the unexplained choice of Orange for the headquarters.

The speaker supported the Regional Investment Corporation Bill 2017, arguing it would establish a corporation to provide direct farm business loans and administer a National Water Infrastructure Loan Facility, aiming to boost agricultural productivity and support regional communities.

Government amendments to the Regional Investment Corporation Bill 2017 were moved to expand the board from three to between three and five members, with corresponding changes to quorum and vacancy provisions. The change responds to submissions such as the National Farmers' Federation's call for a five-member board, while keeping operating costs offset by loan interest.

The speaker opposed transferring the Anti-Dumping Commission to the department, citing the Brumby review’s concerns about investigative powers and integrity standards, and asked how department staff would meet the same thresholds as customs officers. He also reiterated support for reversing the onus of proof in dumping cases.
The speaker moved to introduce the Criminal Code Amendment (Harming Australians) Bill 2013, which amends the Criminal Code Act 1995, and the motion was agreed to.
The Parliamentary Proceedings Broadcasting Amendment Bill 2013 was introduced to amend the Parliamentary Proceedings Broadcasting Act 1946, and the bill was read a first time.

Two bills were introduced: the Parliamentary Proceedings Broadcasting Amendment Bill 2013 and the Commonwealth Electoral Amendment (Above the Line Voting) Bill 2013, with explanatory memoranda tabled.
Commonwealth Electoral Amendment (Above the Line Voting) Bill 2013
The speaker introduced the Commonwealth Electoral Amendment (Above the Line Voting) Bill 2013 to amend the Commonwealth Electoral Act 1918. The bill was agreed to and read a first time.

The Interactive Gambling Amendment (Virtual Credits) Bill 2013 was moved to close a loophole by redefining "gambling service" to include virtual tokens, credits, or coins purchased with real money, citing examples like DoubleDown Casino and Zynga Poker where consumers could not cash out winnings. The amendment aims to improve consumer protection and prevent children’s access to such games.
Criminal Code Amendment (Misrepresentation of Age to a Minor) Bill 2013

The speaker moved to introduce the Criminal Code Amendment (Misrepresentation of Age to a Minor) Bill 2013, which creates new offences for misrepresenting age to minors online under the Criminal Code Act 1995. The bill was agreed to and read a first time.
